---
title: "13_Analysis"
output: html_document
---
```{r}
 library(tidyverse)
 load("12_cleanedElectionData.RData")
```

```{r}
   class_levels <- c("Lower Class", "Working Class", "Middle Class", "Upper Class")

   class_data <- anes_cleaned %>%
     filter(!is.na(social_class)) %>%
     mutate(social_class = factor(social_class, levels = class_levels))

   ggplot(class_data, aes(x = social_class, fill = vote_pres)) +
     geom_bar(position = "fill") +
     scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
     scale_fill_manual(values = c(Democrat = "#2166AC", Republican = "#B2182B")) +
     labs(
       title = "2024 Presidential Vote by Social Class",
       x = "Self-Reported Social Class",
       y = "Share of Respondents",
       fill = "Presidential Vote"
     ) +
     theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
   class_data %>%
     count(social_class, vote_pres) %>%
     group_by(social_class) %>%
     mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

   chisq.test(table(class_data$social_class, class_data$vote_pres))
```

Analysis: Vote choice differed across self-reported social class in this sample, and the association was statistically significant, χ²(3) ≈ 64, p < .001. Working-class respondents were the only group with a Republican majority (51.3%). Republican support was lower among lower-class (43.9%) and middle-class (41.8%) respondents and lowest among upper-class respondents (23.8%). The pattern was not a steady trend across class levels: Republican support rose from the lower class to the working class, then fell at each higher level.

These results show an association, not a causal effect, and social class is self-reported. They are also unweighted and include only respondents who reported voting for a Democratic or Republican presidential candidate, so they should not be generalized to all U.S. voters.

```{r}
age_data <- anes_cleaned %>% filter(!is.na(age))

ggplot(age_data, aes(x = vote_pres, y = age, fill = vote_pres)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Democrat = "#2166AC", Republican = "#B2182B")) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by 2024 Presidential Vote",
    x = "Presidential Vote",
    y = "Age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
age_data %>%
  group_by(vote_pres) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age), median_age = median(age), sd_age = sd(age))

t.test(age ~ vote_pres, data = age_data)
```
Analysis: Republican voters in this sample were slightly older on average than Democratic voters (M = 56.12 vs. 54.86 years), and their median age was also higher (59 vs. 57). A Welch two-sample t-test found this difference statistically significant, t(3290.9) = -2.21, p = .027. The estimated difference was small, however, at about 1.26 years (95% CI [0.14, 2.38], with Republicans older). The boxplot also shows that the two age distributions overlap heavily and have similar spreads, so age alone does not clearly separate the two groups of voters.

This result shows an association, not a causal effect. It is unweighted and excludes respondents with missing age, so it should not be generalized to all U.S. voters.
